classification.difficultyReason: Recall standard angle names and subtract given angles from 90° or 180°.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Classify these angles using the standard terms.

answer.worked: $90^{\circ}<140^{\circ}<180^{\circ}$, so it is an obtuse angle.
An angle of $360^{\circ}$ is a revolution.
$0^{\circ}<33^{\circ}<90^{\circ}$, so it is an acute angle.
An angle of $180^{\circ}$ is a straight angle.
An angle of $90^{\circ}$ is a right angle.
$180^{\circ}<350^{\circ}<360^{\circ}$, so it is a reflex angle.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Write down the complements of:

answer.worked:
Complementary angles add to $90^{\circ}$.
$$90^{\circ}-20^{\circ}=70^{\circ}$$

Complementary angles add to $90^{\circ}$.
$$90^{\circ}-72^{\circ}=18^{\circ}$$

Complementary angles add to $90^{\circ}$.
$$90^{\circ}-45^{\circ}=45^{\circ}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Write down the supplements of:

answer.worked:
Supplementary angles add to $180^{\circ}$.
$$180^{\circ}-20^{\circ}=160^{\circ}$$

Supplementary angles add to $180^{\circ}$.
$$180^{\circ}-172^{\circ}=8^{\circ}$$

Supplementary angles add to $180^{\circ}$.
$$180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}=90^{\circ}$$

content.prompt: This question reviews angles at a point. Find the angles marked with pronumerals, giving reasons.

spec.description: Three rays from A with endpoint labels B, C and D; right-angle square between AC and AD.
spec.mathematics: Angle BAD is 135 degrees; angle CAD is 90 degrees; angle CAB is theta.
spec.answerVisibility: Givens and unknown only.

answer.worked:
Angles in a revolution add to $360^{\circ}$.
$$\begin{align*}\theta+135^{\circ}+90^{\circ}&=360^{\circ}\\\theta+225^{\circ}&=360^{\circ}\\\theta&=135^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Straight lines AB and PQ intersect at M; all four endpoint labels and three angle labels retained.
spec.mathematics: AMQ is alpha; PMA is beta; QMB is 110 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Givens and unknowns only.

answer.worked:
Vertically opposite angles are equal, so $\beta=110^{\circ}$.

Adjacent angles on a straight line are supplementary.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+110^{\circ}&=180^{\circ}\\\alpha&=70^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: K, N and L are collinear; NR and NS form a marked right angle above the line.
spec.mathematics: KNR is alpha; RNS is 90 degrees; SNL is three alpha.
spec.answerVisibility: Givens and unknowns only.

answer.worked:
Adjacent angles on a straight line add to $180^{\circ}$.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+90^{\circ}+3\alpha&=180^{\circ}\\4\alpha&=90^{\circ}\\\alpha&=22\tfrac12^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: AD and BE are straight lines through N, with additional ray NC and a right-angle square between NB and NC.
spec.mathematics: BNC is 90 degrees; CND is 60 degrees; ANE is theta and vertically opposite BND.
spec.answerVisibility: Givens and unknown only.

answer.worked:
$\angle BND=90^{\circ}+60^{\circ}=150^{\circ}$.

Vertically opposite angles are equal, so $\theta=150^{\circ}$.

spec.description: Five unlabelled rays and five consecutive theta labels around their common vertex; source ray directions are schematic.
spec.mathematics: Five equal angles partition one revolution.
spec.answerVisibility: Unknown labels only; no calculated value.

answer.worked:
Angles in a revolution add to $360^{\circ}$.
$$\begin{align*}5\theta&=360^{\circ}\\\theta&=72^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: OP and OS bound a marked right angle, containing rays OQ and OR in that order.
spec.mathematics: POQ is three alpha; QOR is two alpha; ROS is alpha; POS is 90 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Givens and unknowns only.

answer.worked:
The three adjacent angles form a right angle.
$$\begin{align*}3\alpha+2\alpha+\alpha&=90^{\circ}\\6\alpha&=90^{\circ}\\\alpha&=15^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: This question reviews angles across transversals. Find the angles marked with pronumerals, giving reasons.

spec.description: Two parallel oblique lines crossed by a steeper transversal; matching single arrows and all six point labels retained.
spec.mathematics: AB parallel CD; 140 degrees at G and alpha at F are alternate interior angles.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied angle and unknown are visible.

answer.worked:
$$\alpha=140^\circ$$
Alternate angles are equal because $AB\parallel CD$.

spec.description: Two oblique parallels with single arrows and two vertical parallels with double arrows.
spec.mathematics: AB parallel CD and PQ parallel RS; 65 degrees, beta and gamma occupy corresponding upper-right sectors.
spec.answerVisibility: Only 65 degrees, beta and gamma are shown.

answer.worked:
$$\beta=65^\circ$$
Corresponding angles are equal because $AB\parallel CD$.

$$\gamma=\beta=65^\circ$$
Corresponding angles are equal because $PQ\parallel RS$.

spec.description: Open chain VWXYZ with two distinct parallel-mark families.
spec.mathematics: VW parallel XY; WX parallel YZ; angle VWX is 100 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Alpha and beta remain unknown.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+100^\circ&=180^\circ\\\alpha&=80^\circ\end{align*}$$
Co-interior angles are supplementary because $WV\parallel XY$.

$$\beta=\alpha=80^\circ$$
Alternate angles are equal because $WX\parallel YZ$.

spec.description: Quadrilateral NKLM with both pairs of opposite sides marked parallel.
spec.mathematics: NK parallel ML, NM parallel KL; interior angle L is 68 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Alpha, beta and gamma are unknown interior angles.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\beta+68^\circ&=180^\circ\\\beta&=112^\circ\end{align*}$$
Co-interior angles, $NK\parallel ML$.

$$\begin{align*}\alpha+\beta&=180^\circ\\\alpha+112^\circ&=180^\circ\\\alpha&=68^\circ\end{align*}$$
Co-interior angles, $NM\parallel KL$.

$$\begin{align*}\gamma+68^\circ&=180^\circ\\\gamma&=112^\circ\end{align*}$$
Co-interior angles, $NM\parallel KL$.

spec.description: Two oblique parallels with one transversal and co-interior labels.
spec.mathematics: AB parallel CD; theta and 2theta are co-interior angles.
spec.answerVisibility: Neither unknown angle is evaluated.

answer.worked:
Co-interior angles are supplementary because $AB\parallel CD$.

$$\begin{align*}\theta+2\theta&=180^\circ\\3\theta&=180^\circ\\\theta&=60^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Three parallel segments AD, BE and CF, joined by DE and EF.
spec.mathematics: Angle ADE is 50 degrees; angle CFE is 35 degrees; theta is the right-facing angle DEF.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied angles are evaluated.

answer.worked:
$$\angle BED=180^\circ-50^\circ=130^\circ$$
Co-interior angles, $AD\parallel BE$.

$$\angle BEF=180^\circ-35^\circ=145^\circ$$
Co-interior angles, $BE\parallel CF$.

$$\begin{align*}\theta+130^\circ+145^\circ&=360^\circ\\\theta&=85^\circ\end{align*}$$
Angles at a point sum to $360^\circ$.

content.prompt: This question reviews tests for two lines to be parallel. In each part, name all pairs of parallel lines, giving reasons.

spec.description: Z-shaped chain ABCD with no supplied parallel arrows.
spec.mathematics: Angles ABC and BCD are each 37 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Parallelism is not marked.

answer.worked:
$$\angle ABC=\angle BCD=37^\circ$$
These alternate angles are equal, so $AB\parallel CD$.

spec.description: Collinear A, B, C; segments BE and CD descend right; no parallel arrows.
spec.mathematics: Angles ABE and ACD are each 50 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the two supplied angles are shown.

answer.worked:
$$\angle ABE=\angle ACD=50^\circ$$
These corresponding angles are equal, so $BE\parallel CD$.

spec.description: Vertical QR joins two rightward segments; right-angle squares at Q and R.
spec.mathematics: Angles PQR and QRS are right angles.
spec.answerVisibility: No parallel arrows are supplied.

answer.worked:
$$\angle PQR+\angle QRS=90^\circ+90^\circ=180^\circ$$
The co-interior angles are supplementary, so $QP\parallel RS$.

spec.description: Two cross-lines AB and CD crossed by EF and GH; all three supplied angles retained without parallel arrows.
spec.mathematics: The two right-side interior angles on EF are 85 degrees each; the upper-left angle on GH at CD is 100 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: No inferred angle or parallelism is shown.

answer.worked:
$$85^\circ+85^\circ=170^\circ\ne180^\circ$$
The co-interior angles show that $AB$ and $CD$ are not parallel.

$$85^\circ+100^\circ=185^\circ\ne180^\circ$$
The co-interior angles show that $EF$ and $GH$ are not parallel. Each remaining pair intersects in the diagram, so there are no parallel pairs.

spec.description: KLM collinear, NO lower left, OL diagonal and LP descending right.
spec.mathematics: Angle NOL is 130 degrees, OLP is 50 degrees and PLM is 80 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: The angle needed for the parallelism test is not supplied.

answer.worked:
$$\angle OLM=50^\circ+80^\circ=130^\circ$$
Adjacent angles at $L$.

$$\angle NOL=\angle OLM=130^\circ$$
These alternate angles are equal, so $NO\parallel KM$.

spec.description: Quadrilateral ABCD with three supplied interior angles and no parallel markings.
spec.mathematics: A is 95 degrees, B is 80 degrees and D is 85 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Angle C and parallel relationships are not shown.

answer.worked:
$$\angle DAB+\angle ADC=95^\circ+85^\circ=180^\circ$$
These co-interior angles are supplementary, so $AB\parallel DC$.

$$\angle DAB+\angle ABC=95^\circ+80^\circ=175^\circ\ne180^\circ$$
Thus $AD$ and $BC$ are not parallel. The only parallel pair is $AB\parallel DC$.

content.prompt: This question reviews angle sums of triangles and quadrilaterals. Find the angles marked with pronumerals, giving reasons.

spec.description: Triangle ABC with A above BC; all three interior angle labels retained.
spec.mathematics: Angle A is theta, angle B is 80 degrees and angle C is 65 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Givens and theta only.

answer.worked:
The angles of $\triangle ABC$ sum to $180^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\theta+80^\circ+65^\circ&=180^\circ\\\theta&=35^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Quadrilateral KLMN with coordinate-derived right-angle squares at K and M.
spec.mathematics: Angles K and M are 90 degrees, L is 115 degrees and N is alpha.
spec.answerVisibility: Givens and alpha only.

answer.worked:
The angles of quadrilateral $KLMN$ sum to $360^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+90^\circ+115^\circ+90^\circ&=360^\circ\\\alpha&=65^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: P, A and B are collinear. A curved leader identifies the narrow interior angle ACB as 20 degrees.
spec.mathematics: Exterior angle PAC is theta; interior ABC is 110 degrees and ACB is 20 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Givens and theta only.

answer.worked:
An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles of $\triangle ABC$.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=110^\circ+20^\circ\\\theta&=130^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Quadrilateral RSTU and diagonal US, retaining the curved 50-degree leader to the upper angle RUS.
spec.mathematics: URS=110 degrees, RUS=50 degrees, SUT=UST=40 degrees, RSU=alpha and STU=beta.
spec.answerVisibility: All source givens retained; unknowns remain alpha and beta.

answer.short:
$\alpha=20^\circ$, $\beta=100^\circ$.

Use the angle sum in each of $\triangle URS$ and $\triangle UST$.
answer.worked:
In $\triangle URS$, the angles sum to $180^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+110^\circ+50^\circ&=180^\circ\\\alpha&=20^\circ\end{align*}$$
In $\triangle UST$, the angles sum to $180^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\beta+40^\circ+40^\circ&=180^\circ\\\beta&=100^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Unshaded irregular quadrilateral FEHG with each interior angle label retained.
spec.mathematics: F=2theta, E=130 degrees, H=80 degrees and G=theta.
spec.answerVisibility: Givens and symbolic unknowns only.

answer.worked:
The angles of quadrilateral $FEHG$ sum to $360^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}2\theta+130^\circ+80^\circ+\theta&=360^\circ\\3\theta+210^\circ&=360^\circ\\3\theta&=150^\circ\\\theta&=50^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Horizontal A-B-C and perpendicular vertical B-D-E-F, with separate segments AD and CE. All six point labels and the redundant 140-degree given retained.
spec.mathematics: BAD=45 degrees, ABD=90 degrees, ADE=beta and CEF=140 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Source givens and beta only.

answer.worked:
Since $AB\perp BD$, $\angle ABD=90^\circ$. The exterior angle of $\triangle ABD$ equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
$$\begin{align*}\beta&=45^\circ+90^\circ\\\beta&=135^\circ\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: This question reviews isosceles and equilateral triangles. Find the angles and sides marked with pronumerals, giving reasons.

spec.description: Tall isosceles triangle ABC with matching double ticks on AB and BC. Ordinary source-blue marks use house black.
spec.mathematics: AB=BC; angle C=80 degrees; angle A=alpha; angle B=beta.
spec.answerVisibility: Unknown values remain symbolic.

answer.worked:
The base angles of isosceles $\triangle ABC$ are equal, so $\alpha=80^\circ$.

Using the angle sum of $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{align*}\beta&=180^\circ-80^\circ-80^\circ\\\beta&=20^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Left-pointing triangle CAB with equal sides CA and CB. Ordinary source-blue marks use house black.
spec.mathematics: CA=CB; angle C=40 degrees; angles A and B are alpha and beta.
spec.answerVisibility: Unknown values remain symbolic.

answer.worked:
The base angles of isosceles $\triangle ABC$ are equal, so $\alpha=\beta$.

Using the triangle angle sum:
$$\begin{align*}2\alpha+40^\circ&=180^\circ\\2\alpha&=140^\circ\\\alpha&=70^\circ\end{align*}$$
Thus $\beta=70^\circ$.

spec.description: Inverted triangle LMN with two given equal angles and labelled sloping sides. Ordinary source-blue marks use house black.
spec.mathematics: Angles L=M=50 degrees; LN=11; MN=2x+7.
spec.answerVisibility: x remains unknown.

answer.worked:
Equal angles in $\triangle LMN$ have equal opposite sides, so $MN=LN$.
$$\begin{align*}2x+7&=11\\2x&=4\\x&=2\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Triangles PQR and QRS share QR; all four marked segments retain double ticks and Q has a right angle below QR. Ordinary source-blue marks use house black.
spec.mathematics: PQ=PR=QR=QS; angle RQS=90 degrees; angle QPR=alpha; angle QSR=beta.
spec.answerVisibility: Unknown angles remain symbolic.

answer.worked:
$PQ=PR=QR$, so $\triangle PQR$ is equilateral and $\alpha=60^\circ$.

$QR=QS$, so the base angles of right isosceles $\triangle QRS$ are equal.
$$\begin{align*}2\beta+90^\circ&=180^\circ\\2\beta&=90^\circ\\\beta&=45^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Triangle KLM with all three angles labelled alpha and three side expressions. No side ticks are added. Ordinary source-blue marks use house black.
spec.mathematics: All angles equal alpha; KL=3y; KM=x; LM=6.
spec.answerVisibility: All requested values remain symbolic.

answer.worked:
Using the triangle angle sum:
$$\begin{align*}3\alpha&=180^\circ\\\alpha&=60^\circ\end{align*}$$
All three angles are equal, so $\triangle KLM$ is equilateral. Hence $x=6$ and
$$\begin{align*}3y&=6\\y&=2\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Two isosceles triangles share horizontal TU, with double ticks above and triple ticks below. Ordinary source-blue marks use house black.
spec.mathematics: RT=RU; TS=US; angle RTU=50 degrees; angle TUS=70 degrees; unknowns alpha at RUT, beta at UTS, gamma at TSU.
spec.answerVisibility: Unknown angles remain symbolic.

answer.short:
$\alpha=50^\circ$, $\beta=70^\circ$, $\gamma=40^\circ$.

Use the equal base angles in each isosceles triangle, then the triangle angle sum.
answer.worked:
$RT=RU$, so the base angles of isosceles $\triangle TRU$ are equal: $\alpha=50^\circ$.

$TS=US$, so the base angles of isosceles $\triangle STU$ are equal: $\beta=70^\circ$.

Using the angle sum of $\triangle STU$:
$$\begin{align*}\gamma&=180^\circ-70^\circ-70^\circ\\\gamma&=40^\circ\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.mappingNote: Parts a and b use equal base angles and the angle sum; c uses equal angles to equate opposite sides; d uses equilateral and right isosceles triangles; e uses equal angles to establish an equilateral triangle; f combines two isosceles triangles and an angle sum.

content.prompt: Find the values of the pronumerals $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\theta$ and $x$. Different methods are combined in each part of this question.

spec.description: P, Q and R are collinear; their line is parallel to TS. QS and RS have matching double ticks.
spec.mathematics: Angle PTS is 70 degrees, PQS is 140 degrees; unknowns are TPQ, TSQ and QRS.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and unknown labels are visible.

answer.short:
$\alpha=40^\circ$, $\beta=110^\circ$, $\gamma=40^\circ$.

Use parallel-line angles and the equal base angles of $\triangle QRS$.
answer.worked:
Co-interior angles, $PQ\parallel TS$:
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+140^\circ&=180^\circ\\\alpha&=40^\circ\end{align*}$$
Co-interior angles, $PR\parallel TS$:
$$\begin{align*}\beta+70^\circ&=180^\circ\\\beta&=110^\circ\end{align*}$$
Angles on the straight line $PQR$ give $\angle SQR=180^\circ-140^\circ=40^\circ$. Since $QS=RS$, the base angles of $\triangle QRS$ are equal, so $\gamma=40^\circ$.

spec.description: Hourglass figure with AB parallel to CD; A, M, D and B, M, C are collinear.
spec.mathematics: BAM is 50 degrees and CMD is 70 degrees; find MCD.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and theta are visible.

answer.worked:
$\angle AMB=70^\circ$ (vertically opposite angles).

Angle sum of $\triangle ABM$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle ABM+50^\circ+70^\circ&=180^\circ\\\angle ABM&=60^\circ\end{align*}$$
$\theta=60^\circ$ (alternate angles, $AB\parallel CD$).

spec.description: M lies on BA; BM, MA and MO have matching double ticks. No right-angle marker is present.
spec.mathematics: ABO is 35 degrees; find BAO.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied 35-degree angle and alpha are visible.

answer.worked:
$BM=MO$, so $\angle BOM=35^\circ$ (base angles of isosceles $\triangle BMO$).

$\angle OMA=35^\circ+35^\circ=70^\circ$ (exterior angle of $\triangle BMO$).

$MA=MO$, so $\angle MOA=\alpha$ (base angles of isosceles $\triangle MAO$).
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+\alpha+70^\circ&=180^\circ\\2\alpha&=110^\circ\\\alpha&=55^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: P and Q lie on OX and OY; PQ is parallel to XY. Theta is below PQ at Q.
spec.mathematics: XOY is 40 degrees and OXY is 65 degrees; theta is PQY.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied values and theta are visible.

answer.worked:
$\angle OPQ=65^\circ$ (corresponding angles, $PQ\parallel XY$).

Exterior angle of $\triangle OPQ$:
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=40^\circ+65^\circ\\\theta&=105^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: AF is parallel to BCG; AB and BC carry matching double ticks.
spec.mathematics: FAC is 40 degrees; theta is ABC.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied angle and theta are visible.

answer.worked:
$\angle ACB=40^\circ$ (alternate angles, $AF\parallel BG$).

$AB=BC$, so $\angle BAC=40^\circ$ (base angles of isosceles $\triangle ABC$).

Angle sum of $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{align*}\theta+40^\circ+40^\circ&=180^\circ\\\theta&=100^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: ABC and ACD share AC; BC is perpendicular to AC, BA is parallel to CD, and AC equals AD.
spec.mathematics: ACD is 60 degrees; AD is 3x+5 and CD is 2x+4. Unknowns are CAD and ABC and x.
spec.answerVisibility: All supplied labels are visible; no computed values are included.

answer.short:
$\alpha=60^\circ$, $\beta=30^\circ$, $x=-1$.

First establish that $\triangle ACD$ is equilateral.
answer.worked:
$AC=AD$, so $\angle ADC=\angle ACD=60^\circ$ (base angles of isosceles $\triangle ACD$).
$$\begin{align*}\alpha+60^\circ+60^\circ&=180^\circ\\\alpha&=60^\circ\end{align*}$$
Thus $\triangle ACD$ is equilateral.

$\angle BAC=60^\circ$ (alternate angles, $BA\parallel CD$).
$$\begin{align*}\beta+90^\circ+60^\circ&=180^\circ\\\beta&=30^\circ\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$AB\perp PQ$.

The two equal adjacent angles on $PQ$ are each $90^\circ$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}2\alpha&=180^\circ\\\alpha&=90^\circ\end{align*}$$
Adjacent angles on straight line $PQ$ are supplementary. Thus $\angle ABQ=90^\circ$, so $AB\perp PQ$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Prove that $\angle ABP=2\times\angle ABQ$.

spec.description: Vertical PBQ with ray BA descending right.
spec.mathematics: Angle PBA=alpha+30 degrees; angle ABQ=alpha-30 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: No answer shown.

answer.worked:
Adjacent angles on straight line $PQ$ are supplementary.
$$\begin{align*}(\alpha+30^\circ)+(\alpha-30^\circ)&=180^\circ\\2\alpha&=180^\circ\\\alpha&=90^\circ\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\angle ABP&=90^\circ+30^\circ=120^\circ\\\angle ABQ&=90^\circ-30^\circ=60^\circ\end{align*}$$
Hence $\angle ABP=2\times\angle ABQ$.

children.prompt: Prove that $PO\perp QO$.

spec.mathematics: Consecutive angles from OB to OA are beta,beta,alpha,alpha.
spec.answerVisibility: No right-angle mark or answer supplied.

answer.worked:
Angles on straight line $BA$ sum to $180^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}2\alpha+2\beta&=180^\circ\\\alpha+\beta&=90^\circ\\\angle POQ&=\beta+\alpha=90^\circ\end{align*}$$
Therefore $PO\perp QO$.

answer.short:
$AB\parallel DC$.

$\alpha=36^\circ$, so the co-interior angles at $A$ and $D$ sum to $180^\circ$.
answer.worked:
The interior angles of quadrilateral $ABCD$ sum to $360^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}3\alpha+\alpha+4\alpha+2\alpha&=360^\circ\\10\alpha&=360^\circ\\\alpha&=36^\circ\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\angle DAB+\angle ADC&=3\alpha+2\alpha\\\angle DAB+\angle ADC&=5\times36^\circ\\\angle DAB+\angle ADC&=180^\circ\end{align*}$$
Therefore $AB\parallel DC$, since these co-interior angles are supplementary.

answer.worked:
The polygons with $5$, $8$ and $12$ sides divide into $3$, $6$ and $10$ triangles respectively. In each case there are two fewer triangles than sides.

answer.worked:
The triangle angles include the decagon's interior angles and the angles around $O$. The angles around $O$ sum to $360^\circ$.

answer.worked:
Draw a convex hexagon, choose an interior point $O$, and join $O$ to its six vertices.

$6\times180^\circ=1080^\circ$.

$1080^\circ-360^\circ=720^\circ$.

answer.short:

Subtract the full revolution at the interior point from the sum for $n$ triangles.
answer.worked:
Joining an interior point $O$ to all $n$ vertices gives $n$ triangles, with total angle sum $180n^\circ$. Their angles around $O$ sum to $360^\circ$.

Let $S$ be the polygon's interior angle sum.

$\begin{align*}S&=180n^\circ-360^\circ\\S&=180(n-2)^\circ\end{align*}$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence find the sum of the 10 exterior angles.

answer.worked:
The interior-angle sum of the decagon is $(10-2)\times180^\circ=1440^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Exterior-angle sum}&=1800^\circ-1440^\circ\\\text{Exterior-angle sum}&=360^\circ\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Draw a convex hexagon and repeat the process.

answer.short: Interior plus exterior angles: $1080^\circ$. Interior angles: $720^\circ$. Exterior angles: $360^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Draw a convex hexagon, extend each side in the same turning direction and mark the six exterior angles.

Each interior angle and its adjacent exterior angle are supplementary, so the combined sum is $6\times180^\circ=1080^\circ$.

The interior-angle sum is $(6-2)\times180^\circ=720^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Exterior-angle sum}&=1080^\circ-720^\circ\\\text{Exterior-angle sum}&=360^\circ\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Using the same technique, find the sum of the exterior angles of a convex polygon with $n$ sides.

answer.short:
$360^\circ$.

Subtract the interior-angle sum from the total of the $n$ supplementary interior/exterior pairs.
answer.worked:
The $n$ supplementary pairs have combined sum $180n^\circ$. The interior-angle sum is $180(n-2)^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Exterior-angle sum}&=180n^\circ-180(n-2)^\circ\\\text{Exterior-angle sum}&=180n^\circ-180n^\circ+360^\circ\\\text{Exterior-angle sum}&=360^\circ\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$\alpha=72^\circ$, $\beta=72^\circ$, $\gamma=36^\circ$.

answer.worked:
Adjacent angles on a straight line are supplementary.

The angles of $\triangle BCZ$ sum to $180^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}\gamma&=180^\circ-72^\circ-72^\circ\\\gamma&=36^\circ\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Paired right triangles with vertical left legs, horizontal bases and all printed lengths; retain the printed 67-degree given.
spec.mathematics: DE=RS=5 cm, DF=RT=13 cm; right angles E and S; angle D=67 degrees; EF=a cm, ST=b cm.
spec.answerVisibility: a, b, alpha and beta remain unknown.

answer.worked:
Using Pythagoras in $\triangle DEF$:
$$\begin{align*}a^2+5^2&=13^2\\a^2&=169-25\\a^2&=144\\a&=12.\end{align*}$$
$\triangle DEF\equiv\triangle RST$ (RHS), so $b=12$ and $\alpha=67^\circ$ (matching sides and angles).
$$\begin{align*}\beta&=180^\circ-90^\circ-67^\circ\\\beta&=23^\circ.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: $AB$ is a chord of a circle centre $O$ and $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$. Prove that $OM$ is perpendicular to $AB$.

answer.short:
$OM\perp AB$.

By SSS, $\triangle OAM\equiv\triangle OBM$. The matching angles at $M$ are equal and supplementary, so each is $90^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Join $OA$ and $OB$. In triangles $OAM$ and $OBM$:
$$\begin{align*}OA&=OB&&\text{(radii)}\\AM&=BM&&\text{(}M\text{ is the midpoint of }AB\text{)}\\OM&=OM&&\text{(common side)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle OAM\equiv\triangle OBM$ (SSS), so $\angle OMA=\angle OMB$ (matching angles of congruent triangles).

Since $A$, $M$ and $B$ lie on a straight line,
$$\begin{align*}\angle OMA+\angle OMB&=180^\circ\\2\angle OMA&=180^\circ\\\angle OMA&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Hence $OM\perp AB$.

answer.short:
$AB\parallel CD$.

Use SAS to prove $\triangle AOB\equiv\triangle DOC$, then use equal alternate angles.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}OA&=OD &&\text{(radii)}\\OB&=OC &&\text{(radii)}\\\angle AOB&=\angle DOC &&\text{(vertically opposite angles)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle AOB\equiv\triangle DOC$ (SAS).

answer.short:
$\angle ABC=\angle ABD=90^\circ$, so $AB\perp CD$.

Use SAS, matching angles and supplementary angles.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}AB&=AB &&\text{(common side)}\\AC&=AD &&\text{(given)}\\\angle BAC&=\angle BAD &&\text{(given)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle BAC\equiv\triangle BAD$ (SAS).

Hence $\angle ABC=\angle ABD$ (matching angles of congruent triangles). Since $C,B,D$ are collinear, these angles are supplementary.
$$\begin{align*}\angle ABC+\angle ABD&=180^\circ\\2\angle ABC&=180^\circ\\\angle ABC&=90^\circ\end{align*}$$
Thus $\angle ABD=90^\circ$ and $AB\perp CD$.

spec.description: Triangle ABC with angle bisector AR and a right angle at R; ordinary source blue strokes use house black.
spec.mathematics: B, R, C are collinear; AR is perpendicular to BC; angle BAR equals angle RAC.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible.

answer.short: $\triangle ARB\equiv\triangle ARC$ (AAS), so $AB=AC$. Hence $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles.
answer.worked:
In triangles $ARB$ and $ARC$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle BAR&=\angle CAR &&\text{(given)}\\\angle ARB&=\angle ARC=90^\circ &&\text{(perpendicular lines)}\\AR&=AR &&\text{(common side)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle ARB\equiv\triangle ARC$ (AAS). Hence $AB=AC$ (matching sides of congruent triangles), so $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use congruence to prove that $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles, given that $BP=CQ$.

spec.description: Crossing perpendicular segments BP and CQ inside triangle ABC; their intersection remains unlabelled.
spec.mathematics: P lies on AC, Q lies on AB, BP is perpendicular to AC, and CQ is perpendicular to AB.
spec.answerVisibility: No congruence conclusion or additional equal-side marks are supplied.

answer.short: $\triangle BQC\equiv\triangle CPB$ (RHS), giving $\angle QBC=\angle PCB$. Thus $AB=AC$ and $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles.
answer.worked:
In right-angled triangles $BQC$ and $CPB$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle BQC&=\angle CPB=90^\circ &&\text{(given)}\\BC&=CB &&\text{(common hypotenuse)}\\CQ&=BP &&\text{(given)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle BQC\equiv\triangle CPB$ (RHS). Hence $\angle QBC=\angle PCB$ (matching angles). Since $Q$ lies on $AB$ and $P$ lies on $AC$, $\angle ABC=\angle ACB$. Therefore $AB=AC$ (sides opposite equal angles), so $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles.

content.prompt: In each part, $O$ is the centre of the circle or circles. You will need to construct radii and use congruence in these questions.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that $PQ$ bisects $AB$.

spec.description: Circle, horizontal diameter QP and perpendicular vertical chord AB meeting at N; radii OA and OB are intentionally absent.
spec.mathematics: O is the centre, QP is a diameter, N lies on AB and QP, and AB is perpendicular to QP.
spec.answerVisibility: Students construct the needed radii.

answer.short: Construct $OA$ and $OB$. Then $\triangle AON\equiv\triangle BON$ (RHS), giving $AN=BN$; hence $PQ$ bisects $AB$.
answer.worked:
Construct radii $OA$ and $OB$. In triangles $AON$ and $BON$:
$$\begin{align*}OA&=OB &&\text{(radii)}\\ON&=ON &&\text{(common side)}\\\angle ANO&=\angle BNO=90^\circ &&\text{(perpendicular lines)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle AON\equiv\triangle BON$ (RHS). Hence $AN=BN$ (matching sides), so $PQ$ bisects $AB$ at $N$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Prove that $AB=CD$.

spec.description: Two concentric circles intersected by one chord line above O, with intersections A, B, C, D in order. No radii or perpendicular are supplied.
spec.mathematics: OA=OD and OB=OC are available only after students construct radii.
spec.answerVisibility: Only circles, chord, centre point and labels are visible.

answer.short: Construct $OA$, $OB$, $OC$ and $OD$. Equal radii and equal base angles give $\triangle ABO\equiv\triangle DCO$ (AAS), so $AB=CD$.
answer.worked:
Construct $OA$, $OB$, $OC$ and $OD$.
$$\begin{align*}OA&=OD &&\text{(radii of the larger circle)}\\\angle OAD&=\angle ADO &&\text{(base angles of isosceles }\triangle AOD\text{)}\\OB&=OC &&\text{(radii of the smaller circle)}\\\angle OBC&=\angle BCO &&\text{(base angles of isosceles }\triangle BOC\text{)}\end{align*}$$
Since $A,B,C,D$ are collinear:
$$\begin{align*}\angle ABO&=180^\circ-\angle OBC\\\angle DCO&=180^\circ-\angle BCO\end{align*}$$
Thus $\angle ABO=\angle DCO$. Also $\angle BAO=\angle CDO$, since these are the equal base angles of $\triangle AOD$. Together with $OA=OD$, this gives $\triangle ABO\equiv\triangle DCO$ (AAS). Therefore $AB=CD$ (matching sides).

children.label: i
children.prompt: Find the sizes of $\angle B$ and $\angle D$ in terms of $\alpha$.

answer.worked:
$\angle B=180^\circ-\alpha$ because co-interior angles are supplementary when $AD\parallel BC$.

$\angle D=180^\circ-\alpha$ because co-interior angles are supplementary when $AB\parallel DC$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence find the size of $\angle C$ in terms of $\alpha$.

answer.short: $\angle C=\alpha$. Thus opposite angles are equal.
answer.worked:
Using the angle sum of quadrilateral $ABCD$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle C&=360^\circ-\alpha-(180^\circ-\alpha)-(180^\circ-\alpha)\\\angle C&=\alpha.\end{align*}$$
Thus $\angle A=\angle C$ and, from part i, $\angle B=\angle D$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that: A rhombus is a parallelogram.

spec.description: Unshaded rhombus ABCD with vertical diagonal AC and one matching equality tick on each side. Ordinary source blue strokes use house black.
spec.mathematics: AB=BC=CD=DA; AC is supplied. No parallel marks are given.
spec.answerVisibility: Givens only.

answer.short: By SSS, $\triangle ABC\equiv\triangle CDA$. Hence $\angle BAC=\angle DCA$ and $\angle BCA=\angle DAC$. Equal alternate angles give $AB\parallel DC$ and $AD\parallel BC$, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.
answer.worked:
In triangles $ABC$ and $CDA$:
$$\begin{aligned}AB&=CD&&\text{(sides of a rhombus)}\\BC&=DA&&\text{(sides of a rhombus)}\\AC&=CA&&\text{(common side)}\end{aligned}$$
Therefore $\triangle ABC\equiv\triangle CDA$ (SSS).

Hence $\angle BAC=\angle DCA$ and $\angle BCA=\angle DAC$ (matching angles of congruent triangles). Thus $AB\parallel DC$ and $AD\parallel BC$ (equal alternate angles). Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Prove that: The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular, and bisect the vertex angles through which they pass.

Let the diagonals of the rhombus $APBQ$ meet at $M$.

spec.description: Unshaded rhombus APBQ with both diagonals meeting at M and double equality ticks on all four sides. Ordinary source blue strokes use house black.
spec.mathematics: AP=PB=BQ=QA; A,M,B and Q,M,P are collinear. No perpendicular or angle-bisector marks are supplied.
spec.answerVisibility: Givens only.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Prove that $\triangle APB\equiv\triangle AQB$.

answer.worked:
In triangles $APB$ and $AQB$:
$$\begin{aligned}AP&=AQ&&\text{(sides of a rhombus)}\\PB&=QB&&\text{(sides of a rhombus)}\\AB&=AB&&\text{(common side)}\end{aligned}$$
Therefore $\triangle APB\equiv\triangle AQB$ (SSS).

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence prove that $\angle PAM=\angle QAM$.

answer.short: $\angle PAM=\angle QAM$ (matching angles of congruent triangles).
answer.worked: $\angle PAB=\angle QAB$ (matching angles of the congruent triangles in part i). Since $A$, $M$ and $B$ are collinear, $\angle PAM=\angle QAM$.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Prove also that $AM\perp PQ$.

answer.short: $\triangle QAM\equiv\triangle PAM$ (SAS), so $\angle QMA=\angle PMA=90^\circ$. Hence $AM\perp PQ$.
answer.worked:
In triangles $QAM$ and $PAM$:
$$\begin{aligned}AQ&=AP&&\text{(sides of a rhombus)}\\\angle QAM&=\angle PAM&&\text{(part ii)}\\AM&=AM&&\text{(common side)}\end{aligned}$$
Therefore $\triangle QAM\equiv\triangle PAM$ (SAS), so $\angle QMA=\angle PMA$ (matching angles).

These angles lie on the straight line $QP$, so they are supplementary. Hence $\angle QMA=\angle PMA=90^\circ$ and $AM\perp PQ$.

The congruence in part i also shows that $AB$ bisects the angle at $B$. Applying the same SSS argument to triangles $PAQ$ and $PBQ$ shows that $PQ$ bisects the angles at $P$ and $Q$.

children.label: c
children.prompt:
Prove that: The diagonals of a rectangle are equal.

Let $ABCD$ be a rectangle with the diagonals joined.

spec.description: Unshaded horizontal rectangle ABCD with both diagonals, four right-angle squares, single parallel arrows on AB and DC, and double arrows on AD and BC. Ordinary source blue strokes use house black.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Prove that $\triangle ADC\equiv\triangle BCD$.

answer.worked:
In triangles $ADC$ and $BCD$:
$$\begin{aligned}AD&=BC&&\text{(opposite sides of a parallelogram)}\\\angle ADC&=\angle BCD=90^\circ&&\text{(rectangle)}\\DC&=CD&&\text{(common side)}\end{aligned}$$
Therefore $\triangle ADC\equiv\triangle BCD$ (SAS).

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence prove that $AC=BD$.

answer.worked: Since $\triangle ADC\equiv\triangle BCD$, their matching sides $AC$ and $BD$ are equal. Thus the diagonals of the rectangle are equal.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that $\triangle AOP\equiv\triangle BOP$.

answer.worked:
In triangles $AOP$ and $BOP$:
$$\begin{align*}AO&=BO &&\text{(radii of the circle with centre }O\text{)}\\AP&=BP &&\text{(radii of the circle with centre }P\text{)}\\OP&=OP &&\text{(common side)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle AOP\equiv\triangle BOP$ (SSS).

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence prove that $OP$ bisects $\angle AOB$.

answer.short: $\angle AOP=\angle BOP$ (matching angles of congruent triangles), so $OP$ bisects $\angle AOB$.
answer.worked: From part a, $\angle AOP=\angle BOP$ because matching angles of congruent triangles are equal. Thus $OP$ divides $\angle AOB$ into two equal angles, so $OP$ bisects $\angle AOB$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Prove that $\triangle AOM\equiv\triangle BOM$.

answer.short: $\triangle AOM\equiv\triangle BOM$ (SAS): $OA=OB$, $\angle AOM=\angle BOM$ and $OM$ is common.
answer.worked:
In triangles $AOM$ and $BOM$:
$$\begin{align*}OA&=OB &&\text{(radii)}\\\angle AOM&=\angle BOM &&\text{(part b, since }O,M,P\text{ are collinear)}\\OM&=OM &&\text{(common side)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle AOM\equiv\triangle BOM$ (SAS).

children.label: d
children.prompt: Hence prove that $AM=BM$ and $AB\perp OP$.

answer.short:
$AM=BM$ and $AB\perp OP$.

Matching sides give $AM=BM$; the equal adjacent angles at $M$ are supplementary, so each is $90^\circ$.
answer.worked:
From part c, $AM=BM$ and $\angle AMO=\angle BMO$ (matching sides and angles of congruent triangles).

Since $A,M,B$ are collinear,
$$\begin{align*}\angle AMO+\angle BMO&=180^\circ\\2\angle AMO&=180^\circ\\\angle AMO&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Thus $AB\perp OP$. Together with $AM=BM$, this proves that $OP$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.

content.prompt: This question reviews the proofs of the four tests for a quadrilateral to be a parallelogram.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Prove that: If the opposite angles of a quadrilateral are equal, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $\angle A=\angle C=\alpha$ and $\angle B=\angle D=\beta$.

spec.description: Unshaded quadrilateral ABCD with opposite angle labels alpha and beta; ordinary source-blue outlines rendered black under house style.
spec.mathematics: A and C have angle alpha; B and D have angle beta. No parallel or equal-side marks are supplied.
spec.answerVisibility: All labels and edges are permanent givens.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Prove that $\alpha+\beta=180^\circ$.

answer.worked:
The interior angles of quadrilateral $ABCD$ sum to $360^\circ$.

$$\begin{align*}2\alpha+2\beta&=360^\circ\\\alpha+\beta&=180^\circ\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence prove that $AB\parallel DC$ and $AD\parallel BC$.

answer.short: $AB\parallel DC$ and $AD\parallel BC$, since each relevant pair of co-interior angles sums to $180^\circ$.
answer.worked:
$\angle DAB+\angle ADC=\alpha+\beta=180^\circ$, so $AB\parallel DC$ by the converse of the co-interior angle property.

$\angle DAB+\angle ABC=\alpha+\beta=180^\circ$, so $AD\parallel BC$ by the same converse. Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Prove that: If the opposite sides of a quadrilateral are equal, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

Let $RSTU$ be a quadrilateral with $RS=UT$ and $RU=ST$.

spec.description: RSTU with vertical RS and UT, matching double ticks on RS and UT, matching triple ticks on ST and RU, and supplied red dashed diagonal SU. Ordinary outlines and equality marks are black.
spec.mathematics: RS=UT and ST=RU; SU is common to the two triangles.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied diagonal and equality marks remain visible in the question.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Prove that $\triangle RSU\equiv\triangle TUS$.

answer.worked:
In triangles $RSU$ and $TUS$:

$$\begin{align*}RS&=UT&&\text{(given)}\\RU&=ST&&\text{(given)}\\SU&=US&&\text{(common side)}\end{align*}$$

Therefore $\triangle RSU\equiv\triangle TUS$ by SSS.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence prove that $RS\parallel UT$ and $RU\parallel ST$.

answer.short: $RS\parallel UT$ and $RU\parallel ST$, using equal matching angles of congruent triangles and the converse of the alternate angle property.
answer.worked:
$\angle RSU=\angle TUS$ because matching angles of congruent triangles are equal. These are alternate angles on transversal $SU$, so $RS\parallel UT$.

Similarly, $\angle RUS=\angle TSU$, so $RU\parallel ST$. Thus both pairs of opposite sides are parallel and $RSTU$ is a parallelogram.

children.label: c
children.prompt:
Prove that: If one pair of opposite sides of a quadrilateral are equal and parallel, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

Let $KLMN$ be a quadrilateral with $KL=NM$ and $KL\parallel NM$.

spec.description: KLMN with vertical KN and LM, descending KL and NM carrying matching double ticks and single parallel arrows, and a supplied red dashed diagonal KM. Ordinary outlines, ticks and parallel marks are black.
spec.mathematics: KL=NM and KL parallel NM; KM is common to the two triangles.
spec.answerVisibility: All supplied marks and the auxiliary diagonal remain visible.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Prove that $\triangle KLM\equiv\triangle MNK$.

answer.worked:
In triangles $KLM$ and $MNK$:

$$\begin{align*}KL&=MN&&\text{(given)}\\\angle LKM&=\angle NMK&&\text{(alternate angles, }KL\parallel NM\text{)}\\KM&=MK&&\text{(common side)}\end{align*}$$

Therefore $\triangle KLM\equiv\triangle MNK$ by SAS.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence prove that $KN\parallel LM$.

answer.short: $KN\parallel LM$, since $\angle NKM=\angle LMK$ are equal alternate angles.
answer.worked:
$\angle NKM=\angle LMK$ because matching angles of congruent triangles are equal. These are alternate angles on transversal $KM$, so $KN\parallel LM$.

Together with the given $KL\parallel NM$, this proves that $KLMN$ is a parallelogram.

children.label: d
children.prompt:
Prove that: If the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

Let $EFGH$ be a quadrilateral whose diagonals meet at $O$ and bisect each other.

spec.description: Unshaded EFGH with horizontal EF and HG. Solid diagonals EG and HF intersect at O. EO and OG have double ticks; HO and OF have triple ticks. Ordinary source-blue lines and marks are black.
spec.mathematics: EO=OG and HO=OF; E,O,G and H,O,F are collinear.
spec.answerVisibility: Both diagonals, intersection label and all equality marks are supplied givens.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Prove that $\triangle EHO\equiv\triangle GFO$.

answer.worked:
In triangles $EHO$ and $GFO$:

$$\begin{align*}EO&=GO&&\text{(given)}\\HO&=FO&&\text{(given)}\\\angle EOH&=\angle GOF&&\text{(vertically opposite angles)}\end{align*}$$

Therefore $\triangle EHO\equiv\triangle GFO$ by SAS.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence prove that $EH=FG$ and $EH\parallel FG$.

answer.short: $EH=FG$ by matching sides, and $EH\parallel FG$ by equal alternate angles.
answer.worked:
$EH=FG$ because matching sides of congruent triangles are equal.

$\angle HEO=\angle FGO$ because matching angles of congruent triangles are equal. These are alternate angles on transversal $EG$, so $EH\parallel FG$.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Explain why this proves that $EFGH$ is a parallelogram.

answer.short: One pair of opposite sides, $EH$ and $FG$, are equal and parallel, so $EFGH$ is a parallelogram.
answer.worked: Part (ii) establishes that the opposite sides $EH$ and $FG$ are equal and parallel. By the test proved in part (c), $EFGH$ is a parallelogram.

children.label: b

answer.short: Yes. $AM=OB$ and $BM=OA$ by construction, so both pairs of opposite sides of $AMBO$ are equal.

Equal corresponding angles give $AQ\parallel PC$, so $APCQ$ is a parallelogram.

Thus $\angle PAQ=\angle BPC$, so $AQ\parallel PC$ (equal corresponding angles). Since $AP\parallel QC$ as well, $APCQ$ is a parallelogram. Its opposite sides are equal, so $AP=QC$.

children.prompt: Given that $RSTU$ is a parallelogram, prove that $UX\parallel YS$.

spec.mathematics: XS=UY and XS is parallel to UY. Opposite outer sides have paired parallel arrows.
spec.answerVisibility: No requested parallelism marked on UX and YS.

answer.short:
$UX\parallel YS$.

$XS=UY$ and $XS\parallel UY$, so $XSYU$ is a parallelogram.
answer.worked: $XS\parallel UY$ because $RS\parallel UT$. Also $XS=UY$ (given). Thus $XSYU$ is a parallelogram, since one pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel. Its other pair of opposite sides is parallel, so $UX\parallel YS$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram with $X$ and $Y$ points on the diagonal $BD$ such that $BY=DX$. Prove that $AYCX$ is a parallelogram.

spec.description: Outer parallelogram, diagonal DB with D,X,Y,B in order, equal ticks on DX and YB, and dotted target quadrilateral.
spec.mathematics: BY=DX; both pairs of outer opposite sides are parallel.
spec.answerVisibility: No congruence or target-side equality supplied.

answer.short:
$AYCX$ is a parallelogram.

SAS congruence gives $AX=CY$ and $AY=CX$, so both pairs of opposite sides are equal.
answer.worked:
In triangles $ADX$ and $CBY$:
$$\begin{align*}AD&=CB &&\text{(opposite sides of a parallelogram)}\\DX&=BY &&\text{(given)}\\\angle ADX&=\angle CBY &&\text{(alternate angles, }AD\parallel BC\text{)}\end{align*}$$
Thus $\triangle ADX\equiv\triangle CBY$ (SAS), so $AX=CY$.

In triangles $ABY$ and $CDX$, $AB=CD$, $BY=DX$, and $\angle ABY=\angle CDX$ (alternate angles, $AB\parallel CD$). Therefore $\triangle ABY\equiv\triangle CDX$ (SAS), so $AY=CX$.

Both pairs of opposite sides of $AYCX$ are equal; hence $AYCX$ is a parallelogram.

children.label: d
children.prompt: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram and $PB=DQ$. Prove that $AQ=CP$.

spec.description: Parallelogram with D,P,Q,B in order on diagonal DB and joins AQ and PC.
spec.mathematics: PB=DQ is stated in the prompt; opposite outer sides are marked parallel.
spec.answerVisibility: AQ and CP are not marked equal.

answer.worked:
In triangles $ADQ$ and $CBP$:
$$\begin{align*}AD&=CB &&\text{(opposite sides of a parallelogram)}\\DQ&=BP &&\text{(given)}\\\angle ADQ&=\angle CBP &&\text{(alternate angles, }AD\parallel BC\text{)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle ADQ\equiv\triangle CBP$ (SAS), so $AQ=CP$ (matching sides).

children.label: e
children.prompt: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram and $BX$ and $DY$ are perpendicular to $AC$. Prove that $BX=DY$.

spec.description: Parallelogram with diagonal AC and perpendiculars BX and DY; feet derived by projection onto AC.
spec.mathematics: A,X,Y,C are collinear in that order. Right-angle squares occur at X and Y; opposite sides have matching parallel arrows.
spec.answerVisibility: No equality marks on the perpendiculars.

answer.worked:
In triangles $ABX$ and $CDY$:
$$\begin{align*}AB&=CD &&\text{(opposite sides of a parallelogram)}\\\angle BAX&=\angle DCY &&\text{(alternate angles, }AB\parallel CD\text{)}\\\angle BXA&=\angle DYC=90^\circ &&\text{(given perpendiculars)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle ABX\equiv\triangle CDY$ (AAS), so $BX=DY$ (matching sides).

children.label: f
children.prompt: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram with $BP=DQ$. Prove that $APCQ$ is a parallelogram.

spec.description: Parallelogram ABCD with P on AB, Q on DC, and joins AQ and PC.
spec.mathematics: BP=DQ is stated in the prompt. Double arrows pair AB with DC; single arrows pair AD with BC.
spec.answerVisibility: No target-quadrilateral conclusion supplied.

answer.short:
$APCQ$ is a parallelogram.

SAS congruence gives $AQ=CP$ and equal angles that establish $AQ\parallel PC$.
answer.worked:
In triangles $ADQ$ and $CBP$:
$$\begin{align*}AD&=CB &&\text{(opposite sides of a parallelogram)}\\DQ&=BP &&\text{(given)}\\\angle ADQ&=\angle CBP &&\text{(opposite angles of }ABCD\text{)}\end{align*}$$
Thus $\triangle ADQ\equiv\triangle CBP$ (SAS). Hence $AQ=CP$ and $\angle DQA=\angle BPC$ (matching parts).

Also $\angle BPC=\angle PCD$ (alternate angles, $AB\parallel DC$). Therefore $\angle DQA=\angle PCD$, so $AQ\parallel PC$ (equal corresponding angles).

One pair of opposite sides of $APCQ$ is equal and parallel, so $APCQ$ is a parallelogram.

answer.worked: $SM=TM$ (given), $\angle AMS=\angle AMT=90^\circ$ (the diagonals meet at right angles), and $AM=AM$ (common side). Therefore $\triangle AMS\equiv\triangle AMT$ by SAS.

spec.description: RSTU with both diagonals drawn and four matching double ticks, one on each diagonal half. The crossing is unlabelled. No right-angle markers are supplied.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Why is $RSTU$ a parallelogram?

children.label: ii

answer.worked: $US=RT$ (given), $RS=SR$ (common side), and $RU=ST$ (opposite sides of parallelogram $RSTU$). Therefore $\triangle URS\equiv\triangle TSR$ by SSS.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Hence prove that $\angle URS=\angle TSR$.

answer.short: $\angle URS=\angle TSR$ (matching angles of congruent triangles).
answer.worked: Since $\triangle URS\equiv\triangle TSR$, their matching angles are equal. Hence $\angle URS=\angle TSR$.

children.label: iv
children.prompt: Hence prove that $\angle URS=90^\circ$.

answer.short:
$\angle URS=90^\circ$.

The equal co-interior angles sum to $180^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Since $UR\parallel ST$, the co-interior angles satisfy
$$\begin{align*}\angle URS+\angle TSR&=180^\circ\\2\angle URS&=180^\circ\\\angle URS&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
The opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, so $\angle UTS=90^\circ$. Each remaining angle is supplementary to $\angle URS$, so both are also $90^\circ$. Thus $RSTU$ is a rectangle.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that: A parallelogram with one right angle is a rectangle.

answer.short: The adjacent angles are supplementary to the right angle, so they are also $90^\circ$. The remaining angle is $90^\circ$ by the quadrilateral angle sum. Hence the parallelogram is a rectangle.
answer.worked:
Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram with $\angle ABC=90^\circ$.
Since $AB\parallel CD$, co-interior angles give
$$\begin{align*}\angle BCD&=180^\circ-90^\circ\\\angle BCD&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Since $AD\parallel BC$, co-interior angles also give $\angle DAB=90^\circ$.
Using the angle sum of a quadrilateral,
$$\begin{align*}\angle CDA&=360^\circ-90^\circ-90^\circ-90^\circ\\\angle CDA&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
All interior angles of the parallelogram are right angles, so $ABCD$ is a rectangle.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Prove that: If all angles of a quadrilateral are equal, then the quadrilateral is a rectangle.

answer.short: Each angle is $360^\circ\div4=90^\circ$. Supplementary co-interior angles show that both pairs of opposite sides are parallel. Thus the quadrilateral is a parallelogram with four right angles, so it is a rectangle.
answer.worked:
Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with all four interior angles equal. The angle sum of a quadrilateral gives
$$\begin{align*}\angle DAB&=360^\circ\div4\\\angle DAB&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Therefore every interior angle is $90^\circ$.
Since $\angle DAB+\angle ABC=180^\circ$, the converse co-interior angle test gives $AD\parallel BC$.
Since $\angle ABC+\angle BCD=180^\circ$, the same test gives $AB\parallel CD$.
Thus $ABCD$ is a parallelogram whose interior angles are right angles, so it is a rectangle.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Explain why $AFBG$ is a rectangle.

answer.short: $AFBG$ is a parallelogram because its diagonals bisect each other. It has a right angle at $F$, so it is a rectangle.
answer.worked: $AM=BM$ because $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$, and $FM=MG$ by construction. Thus the diagonals $AB$ and $FG$ bisect each other, so $AFBG$ is a parallelogram. Since $\angle AFB=90^\circ$, this parallelogram is a rectangle.

answer.worked:
Since $AFBG$ is a rectangle, $AB=FG$ and its diagonals bisect each other at $M$. Hence

Therefore $AM=BM=FM=GM$.

answer.short: $MF=AM$, so $F$ is one radius from $M$ and lies on the circle.
answer.worked: From part b, $MF=AM$. Every point whose distance from $M$ equals the radius $AM$ lies on the circle. Hence the circle passes through $F$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that the triangles $ABP$, $CBP$, $ADQ$ and $CDQ$ are all congruent.

answer.worked:
The sides of the square give $AB=CB=AD=CD$. Its diagonal bisects the vertex angles, so
$$\angle ABP=\angle CBP=\angle ADQ=\angle CDQ=45^\circ.$$
Also $BP=DQ$ (given), with $BP$ common to the first two triangles and $DQ$ common to the last two. Thus each triangle has two corresponding sides equal and their included angle equal:
$$\triangle ABP\equiv\triangle CBP\equiv\triangle ADQ\equiv\triangle CDQ\quad\text{(SAS)}.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence prove that $APCQ$ is a rhombus.

answer.short: $AP=PC=CQ=QA$ (matching sides of congruent triangles), so $APCQ$ is a rhombus.
answer.worked:
From part a, matching sides of the congruent triangles give
$$AP=CP=AQ=CQ.$$
Thus the four sides of $APCQ$ are equal, so $APCQ$ is a rhombus.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Let $CFBG$ be a kite with $CF=CG$ and $BF=BG$. Let the diagonals $CB$ and $FG$ meet at $M$.

spec.description: Diamond-oriented kite with a longer upper portion, both diagonals, double upper-side ticks and triple lower-side ticks. No perpendicularity or diagonal-bisection marks are supplied.
spec.mathematics: CF=CG; BF=BG; M is the intersection of CB and FG.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Show that $\triangle CBF\equiv\triangle CBG$.

answer.worked:
In triangles $CBF$ and $CBG$:
$$\begin{align*}CF&=CG&&\text{(given)}\\BF&=BG&&\text{(given)}\\CB&=CB&&\text{(common)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle CBF\equiv\triangle CBG$ (SSS).

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence show that $CB$ bisects $\angle FCG$ and $\angle FBG$.

answer.short: $\angle FCB=\angle BCG$ and $\angle FBC=\angle CBG$, so $CB$ bisects both angles.
answer.worked:
Matching angles of the congruent triangles $CBF$ and $CBG$ give
$$\begin{align*}\angle FCB&=\angle BCG,\\\angle FBC&=\angle CBG.\end{align*}$$
Thus $CB$ bisects $\angle FCG$ and $\angle FBG$.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Show that $\triangle CMF\equiv\triangle CMG$.

answer.worked:
In triangles $CMF$ and $CMG$:
$$\begin{align*}CF&=CG&&\text{(given)}\\CM&=CM&&\text{(common)}\\\angle FCM&=\angle GCM&&\text{(part ii; }C,M,B\text{ are collinear)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle CMF\equiv\triangle CMG$ (SAS).

children.label: iv
children.prompt: Hence show that the diagonals are perpendicular.

answer.short: $CB\perp FG$: the equal adjacent angles at $M$ are each $90^\circ$.
answer.worked:
$\angle CMF=\angle CMG$ (matching angles of congruent triangles). Since $F,M,G$ lie on a straight line,
$$\begin{align*}\angle CMF+\angle CMG&=180^\circ,\\2\angle CMF&=180^\circ,\\\angle CMF&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $CB\perp FG$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Conversely, let $AFBG$ be a quadrilateral in which the diagonal $AB$ bisects the diagonal $FG$ and is perpendicular to it. Prove that $AFBG$ is a kite.

spec.description: Quadrilateral AFBG with AB vertical, FG horizontal, equal FM and MG marks and a right-angle square between MA and MG.
spec.mathematics: FM=MG; AB is perpendicular to FG at M. AM and BM are not marked equal.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible.

answer.short:
$AF=AG$ and $BF=BG$, so $AFBG$ is a kite.

Use SAS on the two pairs of triangles meeting at $M$.
answer.worked:
Since $AB$ bisects $FG$ at right angles, $FM=GM$ and all four angles at $M$ are right angles.

In triangles $AMF$ and $AMG$:
$$\begin{align*}FM&=GM&&\text{(given)}\\\angle AMF&=\angle AMG=90^\circ,\\AM&=AM&&\text{(common)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle AMF\equiv\triangle AMG$ (SAS), so $AF=AG$.

In triangles $BMF$ and $BMG$:
$$\begin{align*}FM&=GM&&\text{(given)}\\\angle BMF&=\angle BMG=90^\circ,\\BM&=BM&&\text{(common)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle BMF\equiv\triangle BMG$ (SAS), so $BF=BG$.

Thus $AFBG$ has two pairs of equal adjacent sides and is a kite.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Let $\ell$ be a line and $P$ a point not on the line. Choose two points $A$ and $B$ on $\ell$. Draw an arc with centre $A$ and radius $AP$. Then draw a second arc with centre $B$ and radius $BP$. Let the arcs meet at $M$. Explain why $PM$ is perpendicular to $\ell$.

spec.description: Two arcs with distinct centres A and B on line ell meet at P and M. Their radii differ. The constructed PM line is dashed red; A, B and P have red point markers. No right-angle mark is added.
spec.mathematics: AP=AM and BP=BM; A and B lie on ell; P and M are the two common arc intersections.
spec.answerVisibility: Construction givens are visible; no proof or additional equality marks are supplied.

answer.short: $AP=AM$ and $BP=BM$, so $APBM$ is a kite. Its diagonals $PM$ and $AB$ are perpendicular; hence $PM\perp\ell$.
answer.worked:
$AP=AM$ because both are radii of the circle with centre $A$. Likewise $BP=BM$ because both are radii of the circle with centre $B$.

Thus $APBM$ is a kite. By part a, its diagonals $AB$ and $PM$ are perpendicular. Since $A$ and $B$ lie on $\ell$, $PM\perp\ell$.

content.prompt: $ABCD$ is a straight line such that $AB=BC=CD$ and $BCPQ$ is a rhombus. The lines produced through $AQ$ and $DP$ meet at $R$. Prove that $\angle ARD$ is a right angle.

spec.description: Triangle ARD enclosing rhombus BCPQ; equal-segment double ticks retained. Ordinary source blue becomes black.
spec.mathematics: A,B,C,D collinear in order; AB=BC=CD=BQ=QP=PC; Q on AR and P on RD.
spec.answerVisibility: Givens only; auxiliary diagonals are introduced in the solution.

answer.short:
$\angle ARD=90^\circ$.

The rhombus diagonals are respectively parallel to $AR$ and $DR$, and are perpendicular.
answer.worked:
Draw the diagonals $BP$ and $CQ$ of the rhombus.

Since $AB=BQ$, $\angle AQB=\angle QAB$. The exterior-angle theorem in $\triangle ABQ$ gives $\angle QBC=2\angle QAB$.

The diagonal $BP$ bisects $\angle QBC$, so $\angle PBC=\angle QAB$. Hence $BP\parallel AQ$ by equal corresponding angles.

Similarly, $CP=CD$ gives $\angle CPD=\angle PDC$, and $\angle BCP=2\angle PDC$. Since $CQ$ bisects $\angle BCP$, $\angle BCQ=\angle PDC$, so $CQ\parallel DP$.

The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular, so $BP\perp CQ$. Therefore $AR\perp DR$ and $\angle ARD=90^\circ$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: The trapezium $ABCD$ has $AB\parallel CD$, $\angle C=70^\circ$ and $\angle D=50^\circ$. Find the sizes of $\angle A$ and $\angle B$.

answer.worked:
Co-interior angles on the parallel lines $AB$ and $CD$ are supplementary:
$$\begin{align*}\angle A&=180^\circ-50^\circ\\\angle A&=130^\circ\\\angle B&=180^\circ-70^\circ\\\angle B&=110^\circ.\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: If the non-parallel sides of a trapezium are equal, then the figure is called an
Prove that the base angles of an isosceles trapezium are equal.

answer.short:
For $AB\parallel DC$ and $AD=BC$, $\angle ADC=\angle BCD$ and $\angle DAB=\angle ABC$.

Construct a parallelogram inside the trapezium and use an isosceles triangle.
answer.worked:
Name the isosceles trapezium $ABCD$, with $AB\parallel DC$ and $AD=BC$. Take $DC$ as the longer base. Draw $BK\parallel AD$ meeting $DC$ at $K$.

$ABKD$ is a parallelogram, so $BK=AD=BC$. Thus $\triangle BKC$ is isosceles and $\angle BKC=\angle BCK$.

Since $BK\parallel AD$, $\angle BKC=\angle ADC$. Also $\angle BCK=\angle BCD$. Therefore $\angle ADC=\angle BCD$.

The angles on each non-parallel side are supplementary because $AB\parallel DC$. Subtracting the equal lower base angles from $180^\circ$ gives $\angle DAB=\angle ABC$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Prove that the diagonals of an isosceles trapezium are equal in length.

answer.short: $DB=AC$ by SAS congruence of $\triangle DBC$ and $\triangle CAD$.
answer.worked:
Name the isosceles trapezium $ABCD$, with $AB\parallel DC$ and $AD=BC$.

In $\triangle DBC$ and $\triangle CAD$:
$$\begin{align*}BC&=AD &&\text{(given)}\\DC&=CD &&\text{(common)}\\\angle BCD&=\angle ADC &&\text{(equal base angles).}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle DBC\equiv\triangle CAD$ by SAS, so $DB=CA$ by matching sides.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Prove that if a trapezium has equal diagonals then it is isosceles.

answer.short:
$AD=BC$, so the trapezium is isosceles.

Use perpendicular heights and RHS congruence, then SAS congruence.
answer.worked:
Name the trapezium $ABCD$, with $AB\parallel DC$ and $DB=AC$. Take $DC$ as the longer base. Draw perpendiculars $AX$ and $BY$ to the line $DC$.

$AX=BY$ because they are perpendicular distances between the same parallel lines. In the right triangles $DBY$ and $CAX$, $DB=CA$ and $BY=AX$, so $\triangle DBY\equiv\triangle CAX$ by RHS. Hence $DY=CX$.

The perpendicular projections $X,Y$ occur in the same direction along the base as $A,B$, with $XY=AB<DC$. If $X$ were at or beyond $D$ on the outside, then $CX>DY$; if $Y$ were at or beyond $C$ on the outside, then $DY>CX$. Thus both feet lie inside $DC$.

Matching angles of the RHS triangles give $\angle BDY=\angle ACX$. Since $DY$ points towards $C$ and $CX$ points towards $D$, $\angle BDC=\angle ACD$.

Now $DB=CA$, $DC=CD$, and $\angle BDC=\angle ACD$, so $\triangle BDC\equiv\triangle ACD$ by SAS. Therefore $BC=AD$ by matching sides, and the trapezium is isosceles.

answer.short:
$NT=UT$.

$\triangle NMT\equiv\triangle UOT$ by AAS, so matching sides are equal.
answer.worked:
In triangles $NMT$ and $UOT$:
$$\begin{align*}MT&=OT &&\text{(given)}\\\angle MNT&=\angle OUT &&\text{(given)}\\\angle NTM&=\angle UTO &&\text{(vertically opposite angles)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle NMT\equiv\triangle UOT$ (AAS).

Hence $NT=UT$ (matching sides of congruent triangles).

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that $\triangle BDC$ is congruent to $\triangle CEB$.

answer.short: $\triangle BDC\equiv\triangle CEB$ (AAS): equal right angles, equal base angles and common side $BC$.
answer.worked:
In $\triangle BDC$ and $\triangle CEB$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle BDC&=\angle CEB=90^\circ &&\text{(perpendicular lines)}\\\angle DCB&=\angle EBC &&\text{(base angles of isosceles }\triangle ABC\text{)}\\BC&=CB &&\text{(common side)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle BDC\equiv\triangle CEB$ (AAS).

children.label: b
children.prompt: Prove that $\triangle AED$ is isosceles.

answer.short:
$AE=AD$, so $\triangle AED$ is isosceles.

Subtract the equal corresponding sides $BE=CD$ from $AB=AC$.
answer.worked:
From part a, $BE=CD$ (matching sides of congruent triangles). Since $E$ lies on $AB$ and $D$ lies on $AC$:
$$\begin{align*}AE&=AB-BE\\AD&=AC-CD.\end{align*}$$
But $AB=AC$ (given) and $BE=CD$, so $AE=AD$. Therefore $\triangle AED$ is isosceles.

answer.short:
$\angle ABC=\angle FED$.

Join $BE$ and add the two pairs of equal alternate angles.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Prove that $ACDF$ is a parallelogram.

answer.short:
$ACDF$ is a parallelogram.

Congruence gives $AC=DF$ and $AC\parallel DF$.
answer.worked: In triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$, $AB=DE$ and $BC=EF$ (given), and $\angle ABC=\angle DEF$ (part a). Thus $\triangle ABC\equiv\triangle DEF$ (SAS). Hence $AC=DF$ and $\angle BAC=\angle EDF$ (matching parts). Since $AB\parallel DE$, these equal angles give $AC\parallel DF$. Therefore $ACDF$ has one pair of opposite sides equal and parallel, so it is a parallelogram.

content.prompt: In a parallelogram $ABCD$, the point $E$ lies on the side $DC$ such that $EA$ bisects $\angle BAD$ and $EB$ bisects $\angle ABC$. Prove that:

spec.description: Parallelogram ABCD with E on DC and segments AE and BE; both parallel-side pairs marked.
spec.mathematics: AB parallel DC and AD parallel BC; EA and EB are angle bisectors as stated in the prompt.
spec.answerVisibility: Givens only.

children.label: a
children.prompt: $DE=EC$

answer.short:
$DE=EC$.

The angle bisectors give $DE=AD$ and $EC=BC$, and $AD=BC$.
answer.worked:
Since $AB\parallel DC$, $\angle BAE=\angle AED$ (alternate angles). Also $\angle DAE=\angle BAE$ because $AE$ bisects $\angle BAD$. Thus $\angle DAE=\angle AED$, so $DE=AD$ (equal angles in $\triangle ADE$).
Similarly, $\angle ABE=\angle BEC$ and $\angle ABE=\angle EBC$, so $EC=BC$ (equal angles in $\triangle BEC$). Since $AD=BC$ (opposite sides of a parallelogram), $DE=EC$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: $DC=2CB$

answer.worked:
From part a, $DE=EC$ and $EC=CB$.
$$\begin{align*}DC&=DE+EC\\DC&=2EC\\DC&=2CB.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: $\angle AEB$ is a right angle

answer.short:
$\angle AEB=90^\circ$.

The bisectors halve supplementary adjacent angles.
answer.worked:
$\angle BAD+\angle ABC=180^\circ$ (co-interior angles, $AD\parallel BC$). Since $AE$ and $BE$ bisect these angles,
$$\begin{align*}\angle EAB+\angle ABE&=\tfrac12(\angle BAD+\angle ABC)\\\angle EAB+\angle ABE&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\angle AEB=180^\circ-90^\circ=90^\circ$ (angle sum of $\triangle AEB$).

inlines.text: If the diagonals of a quadrilateral are perpendicular, then the sums of the squares of opposite sides are equal.
The diagonals of the convex quadrilateral
, to the right, meet at right angles at

spec.description: Unshaded convex quadrilateral with perpendicular diagonals AC and DB meeting at M; right-angle square in the upper-right sector.
spec.mathematics: AC perpendicular to DB at M. All four sides and both diagonals are supplied.
spec.answerVisibility: All geometry and labels are permanent givens; no answer is displayed.

answer.short:
$AB^2+CD^2=AD^2+BC^2$.

Apply Pythagoras’ theorem to the four right-angled triangles at $M$.
answer.worked:
Let $AM=a$, $BM=b$, $CM=c$ and $DM=d$. By Pythagoras’ theorem,
$$\begin{align*}AB^2&=a^2+b^2,\\BC^2&=b^2+c^2,\\CD^2&=c^2+d^2,\\AD^2&=a^2+d^2.\end{align*}$$
Hence
$$\begin{align*}AB^2+CD^2&=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2,\\AD^2+BC^2&=a^2+d^2+b^2+c^2.\end{align*}$$
Both sums contain the same four terms, so $AB^2+CD^2=AD^2+BC^2$.

inlines.text: If the sums of the squares of opposite sides of a quadrilateral are equal, then the diagonals are perpendicular.

spec.description: Unshaded convex quadrilateral with horizontal DB, distinct displayed feet P and Q in order D,P,Q,B, perpendiculars AP and CQ, and both right-angle squares. AC is not drawn.
spec.mathematics: AP and CQ are perpendicular to BD. Distinct feet illustrate the configuration before proving coincidence.
spec.answerVisibility: Permanent source construction only; the requested coincidence is not drawn.

answer.short:
$P=Q$, so $AC\perp BD$.

Pythagoras’ theorem and the given equality force $PQ=0$.
answer.worked:
For the displayed order, let $AP=a$, $BQ=b$, $CQ=c$, $DP=d$ and $PQ=t$. By Pythagoras’ theorem,
$$\begin{align*}AB^2&=a^2+(b+t)^2,\\BC^2&=b^2+c^2,\\CD^2&=c^2+(d+t)^2,\\AD^2&=a^2+d^2.\end{align*}$$
Substitute in the given equality and cancel common terms:
$$\begin{align*}a^2+(b+t)^2+c^2+(d+t)^2&=a^2+d^2+b^2+c^2,\\2t^2+2bt+2dt&=0,\\2t(t+b+d)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Since $t+b+d=BD>0$, $t=0$. Thus $P$ and $Q$ coincide. Both $A$ and $C$ lie on the perpendicular to $BD$ through this common foot, so $AC\perp BD$.

The conclusion also covers other foot positions: take directed distances $DP=x$, $DQ=y$ and let $BD=L>0$. Pythagoras’ theorem gives
$$\begin{align*}AB^2+CD^2-AD^2-BC^2&=(L-x)^2+y^2-x^2-(L-y)^2,\\AB^2+CD^2-AD^2-BC^2&=2L(y-x).\end{align*}$$
The given equality therefore gives $y=x$, so the feet coincide.

children.label: c
children.prompt: What happens if the quadrilateral is non-convex?

answer.short: Parts a and b still hold. For a non-convex quadrilateral, perpendicular diagonals means that the lines containing the diagonals are perpendicular.
answer.worked:
Both results still hold, using the lines containing the diagonals when their intersection lies outside a diagonal segment.

For part a, let these lines meet at $M$. Pythagoras’ theorem still gives
$$\begin{align*}AB^2+CD^2&=AM^2+BM^2+CM^2+DM^2,\\AD^2+BC^2&=AM^2+DM^2+BM^2+CM^2.\end{align*}$$
Thus the sums are equal even when $M$ lies on an extension.

For the converse, the directed-distance calculation in part b remains valid for a non-convex quadrilateral. Since $BD>0$, equality of the sums forces the perpendicular feet to coincide, so the lines $AC$ and $BD$ are perpendicular.

inlines.text: The circle passing through all three vertices of a triangle is called a
The following theorem not only shows that every triangle has a unique circumcircle, but also shows how to construct the circumcircle.
The three perpendicular bisectors of a triangle are concurrent. Their point of intersection (called the circumcentre) is the centre of a circle (called a circumcircle).
Prove this theorem using congruence. In the diagram, the midpoints of

spec.description: Triangle ABC with midpoint ticks in three distinct groups, perpendicular segments OR and OQ marked by right-angle squares, and OP unmarked at P. Red dashed OA, OB and OC distinguish the proposed radii. Ordinary source-blue geometry is black in house style.
spec.mathematics: P, Q and R bisect BC, CA and AB respectively; OR is perpendicular to AB and OQ is perpendicular to CA. Perpendicularity of OP to BC is to be proved.
spec.answerVisibility: All supplied geometry is permanent; no inferred right-angle mark is added at P.

answer.short:
$OA=OB=OC$ by SAS congruence at $R$ and $Q$. SSS congruence gives $\angle BPO=\angle CPO=90^\circ$, so the third perpendicular bisector also passes through $O$.

The circle with centre $O$ and radius $OA$ passes through all three vertices; its centre is uniquely determined by the perpendicular bisectors.
answer.worked:
Let the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $AC$ meet at $O$.

In $\triangle ARO$ and $\triangle BRO$:
$$\begin{align*}AR&=BR &&\text{(midpoint)}\\\angle ARO&=\angle BRO=90^\circ &&\text{(perpendicular bisector)}\\OR&=OR &&\text{(common)}\end{align*}$$
Thus $\triangle ARO\equiv\triangle BRO$ (SAS), so $OA=OB$ (matching sides).

In $\triangle AQO$ and $\triangle CQO$:
$$\begin{align*}AQ&=CQ &&\text{(midpoint)}\\\angle AQO&=\angle CQO=90^\circ &&\text{(perpendicular bisector)}\\OQ&=OQ &&\text{(common)}\end{align*}$$
Thus $\triangle AQO\equiv\triangle CQO$ (SAS), so $OA=OC$ (matching sides). Hence $OA=OB=OC$.

In $\triangle BPO$ and $\triangle CPO$:
$$\begin{align*}BP&=CP &&\text{(midpoint)}\\OB&=OC &&\text{(proved above)}\\OP&=OP &&\text{(common)}\end{align*}$$
Thus $\triangle BPO\equiv\triangle CPO$ (SSS), so $\angle BPO=\angle CPO$ (matching angles). These adjacent angles form a straight angle, so each is $90^\circ$. Therefore $OP\perp BC$.

All three perpendicular bisectors pass through $O$, so they are concurrent. Since $OA=OB=OC$, the circle with centre $O$ and radius $OA$ passes through $A$, $B$ and $C$.

Any circumcentre must lie on the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $AC$, which have only one intersection. Therefore the circumcentre, and hence the circumcircle, is unique.

children.label: a
children.prompt: In each diagram below, imagine that you started at the point $X$, facing $A$, and walked around the figure back to $X$, passing through the vertices $A$, $B$, $C$, … in alphabetical order. Through how many complete revolutions would you turn during your journey? Count clockwise rotation as negative, and anticlockwise revolutions as positive.

spec.description: Triangle ABC with X on CA and an initial travel arrow towards A. Ordinary source blue outlines become black; the starting point and travel direction retain distinct standard accents.

spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens; no turning result shown.

answer.worked: The turns at $A$, $B$ and $C$ are all anticlockwise and together make one complete turn. The total signed turn is $+360^\circ$, so the journey gives $+1$ revolution.

spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens; no turning result shown.

answer.worked: Every vertex produces a clockwise turn. Together these turns make one complete clockwise revolution: a signed turn of $-360^\circ$, or $-1$ revolution.

spec.description: Crossed quadrilateral ABCD with BC crossing DA, no vertex or dot at the crossing, and X on DA below the crossing.
spec.mathematics: Traverse X–A–B–C–D–X. Oppositely oriented loops give cancelling signed turns.

answer.worked: The anticlockwise turns at $A$ and $B$ are cancelled by the clockwise turns at $C$ and $D$. Continue straight through the crossing each time; it is not a vertex. The net signed turn is $0^\circ$, giving $0$ revolutions.

spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens; no turning result shown.

answer.worked: Following the vertices in order produces an anticlockwise turn at every vertex. The outer circuit and the small interior loop together give two complete anticlockwise turns. Continue straight through the crossing. The total signed turn is $+720^\circ$, or $+2$ revolutions.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use these ideas to develop a proof that the sum of the exterior angles of a convex polygon is $360^\circ$.

answer.short: Walking once around a convex polygon turns you through one complete revolution. Each turn is an exterior angle, so their sum is $360^\circ$.
answer.worked: Walk anticlockwise once around the boundary of a convex polygon. At each vertex, the change in direction is the exterior angle there. Convexity means every turn is anticlockwise. Over one circuit, your direction makes exactly one complete revolution and returns to its starting direction. Therefore the sum of the exterior angles is $360^\circ$.

content.prompt: Suppose that you make a journey on the surface of the globe. You start facing east at Singapore, which lies on the Equator. Then you walk east one-quarter of the way around the globe, then turn $90^{\circ}$ north and walk to the North Pole, then turn $90^{\circ}$ towards Singapore and walk back to Singapore, and finally turn facing east just as you started. Through how many revolutions have you turned during this journey, and what is the sum of the exterior angles of your triangular path? Count clockwise turns as negative and anticlockwise turns as positive.

inlines.text: of a positive revolution; exterior-angle sum
The three local turns are each anticlockwise through a right angle.

answer.worked:
The turn from east to north is $90^{\circ}$ anticlockwise. At the North Pole, the return meridian to Singapore is a quarter-turn from the incoming meridian, so this turn is also $90^{\circ}$ anticlockwise. On returning to Singapore, you face south; turning to face east is another $90^{\circ}$ anticlockwise.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Total turn}&=90^{\circ}+90^{\circ}+90^{\circ}\\\text{Total turn}&=270^{\circ}\\\text{Number of revolutions}&=\frac{270^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}}\\\text{Number of revolutions}&=\frac34.\end{align*}$$

Thus you turn through $\tfrac34$ of a positive revolution, and the sum of the exterior angles is $270^{\circ}$. The path lies on a sphere, so the exterior-angle sum for a convex plane polygon does not apply.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that: If the quadrilateral is a trapezium, then a pair of opposite triangles have equal area.

answer.short:
The opposite triangles $ABX$ and $DCX$ have equal area, where $BC\parallel AD$ and the diagonals meet at $X$.

Triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$ have equal areas; subtract their common triangle $AXD$.
answer.worked:
Label the trapezium $ABCD$ in order, with $BC\parallel AD$, and let its diagonals meet at $X$. Write $\lbrack PQR\rbrack$ for the area of triangle $PQR$.

Triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$ share base $AD$ and have the same perpendicular height $h$, since $BC\parallel AD$.

$$\begin{align*}\lbrack ABD\rbrack&=\tfrac12 AD\times h\\\lbrack ACD\rbrack&=\tfrac12 AD\times h\\\lbrack ABX\rbrack+\lbrack AXD\rbrack&=\lbrack DCX\rbrack+\lbrack AXD\rbrack\\\lbrack ABX\rbrack&=\lbrack DCX\rbrack\end{align*}$$

Thus a pair of opposite triangles have equal area.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Conversely, prove that: If a pair of opposite triangles have equal area, then the quadrilateral is a trapezium.

answer.short:
$BC\parallel AD$, so $ABCD$ is a trapezium.

Add the common triangle $AXD$ to the equal opposite triangles. The resulting triangles share base $AD$, so their equal areas give equal perpendicular heights.
answer.worked:
Label the convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ in order and its diagonal intersection $X$, choosing the labels so that $\lbrack ABX\rbrack=\lbrack DCX\rbrack$, where brackets denote triangle areas.

Adding the area of triangle $AXD$ gives

$$\begin{align*}\lbrack ABX\rbrack+\lbrack AXD\rbrack&=\lbrack DCX\rbrack+\lbrack AXD\rbrack\\\lbrack ABD\rbrack&=\lbrack ACD\rbrack.\end{align*}$$

Let $BY$ and $CZ$ be the perpendicular heights from $B$ and $C$ to the line $AD$. The triangles share base $AD$, so

$$\begin{align*}\tfrac12 AD\times BY&=\tfrac12 AD\times CZ\\BY&=CZ.\end{align*}$$

Since the quadrilateral is convex, $B$ and $C$ lie on the same side of $AD$. Their equal perpendicular distances from $AD$ place them on a line parallel to $AD$. Thus $BC\parallel AD$, and $ABCD$ is a trapezium.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Let $ABCD$ be a square. Let $Q$ be a point on $DC$ and $R$ a point on $BC$, and let $AQ\perp DR$. Prove that $AQ=DR$.

answer.short:
$AQ=DR$.

The right-angled triangles $DAQ$ and $CDR$ are congruent by AAS.
answer.worked:
Let $\angle DAQ=\alpha$ and let $M$ be the intersection of $AQ$ and $DR$.

In $\triangle ADQ$, $\angle AQD=90^{\circ}-\alpha$. Since $AQ\perp DR$, the angle sum of $\triangle DMQ$ gives
$$\begin{align*}\angle MDQ&=90^{\circ}-(90^{\circ}-\alpha)\\\angle MDQ&=\alpha.\end{align*}$$
Thus $\angle CDR=\angle DAQ$.

In triangles $DAQ$ and $CDR$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle ADQ&=\angle DCR=90^{\circ}\\\angle DAQ&=\angle CDR\\DA&=CD.\end{align*}$$
The right angles and equal sides are properties of the square. Therefore $\triangle DAQ\equiv\triangle CDR$ by AAS, so $AQ=DR$ as matching sides.

If $Q=D$, perpendicularity gives $R=C$, and both intervals are sides of the square.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Let $ABCD$ be a square. Let $\ell$ and $m$ be perpendicular lines such that $\ell$ intersects the sides $AB$ and $CD$ of the square, and $m$ intersects the sides $AD$ and $BC$. Show that the intervals cut off on $\ell$ and $m$ by the square are equal in length.

answer.short:
The two intervals have equal lengths.

Translate them to the configuration in part a; translation preserves length and perpendicularity.
answer.worked:
Write the square with $A$ at the upper left, $B$ at the upper right, $C$ at the lower right and $D$ at the lower left. Let $E=\ell\cap AB$, $F=\ell\cap CD$, $G=m\cap AD$ and $H=m\cap BC$.

First suppose $EF$ slopes downwards to the right. Translate $EF$ horizontally until $E$ coincides with $A$, and call the image of $F$ point $Q$. The horizontal displacement from $E$ to $F$ lies between zero and the side length, so $Q$ lies on $DC$. Hence $AQ=EF$.

Since $GH\perp EF$, $GH$ slopes upwards to the right. Translate $GH$ vertically until $G$ coincides with $D$, and call the image of $H$ point $R$. The vertical displacement from $G$ to $H$ lies between zero and the side length, so $R$ lies on $BC$. Hence $DR=GH$.

Translations preserve directions, so $AQ\perp DR$. Part a gives $AQ=DR$, and therefore $EF=GH$.

If $EF$ slopes downwards to the left, reflect the entire configuration in the vertical symmetry axis of the square and apply the same argument. Reflection preserves lengths and perpendicularity. If $EF$ is vertical, $GH$ is horizontal and both lengths equal the side length of the square.
