children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that $EFGH$ is a square, and find its area.

answer.short:
$EFGH$ is a square with side length $\sqrt{5}$ and area $5$ square units.

The four outer right triangles are congruent by SAS; their matching sides and complementary acute angles establish the square.
answer.worked:
The extensions give $AE=BF=CG=DH=2$. Also $AH=BE=CF=DG=1$, and the included angles at $A,B,C,D$ are right angles. Therefore
$$\triangle HAE\equiv\triangle BEF\equiv\triangle CFG\equiv\triangle DGH\quad\text{(SAS)}.$$
Matching hypotenuses give $HE=EF=FG=GH$.

At $E$, the ray $EA$ lies inside $\angle HEF$, and $EA$ and $EB$ are the same ray. Hence
$$\begin{align*}\angle HEF&=\angle HEA+\angle BEF\\\angle HEF&=\angle BFE+\angle BEF\\\angle HEF&=90^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$
Here $\angle HEA=\angle BFE$ by congruence, and the acute angles of the right triangle $BEF$ sum to $90^{\circ}$. The same argument at $F,G,H$ gives three further right angles. Thus $EFGH$ has four equal sides and four right angles, so it is a square.

By Pythagoras’ theorem in $\triangle BEF$,
$$\begin{align*}EF^2&=BE^2+BF^2\\EF^2&=1^2+2^2\\EF^2&=5.\end{align*}$$
Thus $EF=\sqrt{5}$ and the area of $EFGH$ is $EF^2=5$ square units.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that the centre $O$ of $ABCD$ is also the centre of $EFGH$.

answer.short:
$O$ is also the centre of $EFGH$.

SAS congruence gives $OE=OF=OG=OH$, placing $O$ on both perpendicular bisectors of the outer square’s diagonals.
answer.worked:
Join $O$ to $E,F,G,H$. Since $O$ is the intersection of the diagonals of $ABCD$, the square’s diagonal properties give
$$OA=OB=OC=OD.$$
Each diagonal makes an angle of $45^{\circ}$ with a side, so
$$\angle OAE=\angle OBF=\angle OCG=\angle ODH=45^{\circ}.$$
Also $AE=BF=CG=DH=2$. Therefore
$$\triangle OAE\equiv\triangle OBF\equiv\triangle OCG\equiv\triangle ODH\quad\text{(SAS)},$$
and matching sides give
$$OE=OF=OG=OH.$$
In particular, $OE=OG$, so $O$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $EG$; likewise $OF=OH$ puts $O$ on the perpendicular bisector of $FH$. In the square $EFGH$, each diagonal is the perpendicular bisector of the other. Consequently $O$ lies on both $EG$ and $FH$, at their intersection. Thus $O$ is the centre of $EFGH$.

content.prompt: Prove that: Any line through the intersection of the diagonals of a parallelogram dissects the parallelogram into two figures of equal area.

answer.short:
The two figures have equal area.

Diagonal bisection and congruent triangles show that the two resulting trapezia have equal parallel sides and the same height.
answer.worked:
Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram whose diagonals intersect at $O$. First suppose the line meets opposite sides $AB$ and $CD$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively, away from the vertices.

The diagonals bisect each other, so $AO=CO$. Also, $\angle AOE=\angle COF$ (vertically opposite angles) and $\angle OAE=\angle OCF$ (alternate angles, $AB\parallel CD$). Therefore $\triangle AOE\equiv\triangle COF$ (AAS), giving $AE=CF$.

Opposite sides of the parallelogram are equal, so $AB=CD$. Hence
$$\begin{align*}EB&=AB-AE\\EB&=CD-CF\\EB&=FD.\end{align*}$$
Let $h$ be the perpendicular distance between $AB$ and $CD$. The two trapezia have areas
$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{area}(AEFD)&=\frac12(AE+FD)h,\\\operatorname{area}(EBCF)&=\frac12(EB+CF)h.
\end{align*}$$
Since $AE=CF$ and $FD=EB$, these areas are equal. The same argument applies if the line meets $AD$ and $BC$, after relabelling the vertices.

If the line passes through a vertex, it is a diagonal. Each diagonal divides the parallelogram into two congruent triangles (SSS, using equal opposite sides and the common diagonal), so their areas are equal. Thus every line through $O$ gives two figures of equal area.

content.prompt: Prove that: The perpendicular bisector of the base of an isosceles triangle passes through its vertex.

answer.short: Join the vertex to the midpoint of the base. The resulting triangles are congruent by SSS, so the two angles at the midpoint are equal and each is $90^{\circ}$. This line is therefore the perpendicular bisector and passes through the vertex.
answer.worked:
Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB=AC$ and base $BC$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and join $AM$.

In triangles $ABM$ and $ACM$:
$$\begin{align*}AB&=AC &&\text{(isosceles triangle)}\\BM&=CM &&\text{(midpoint)}\\AM&=AM &&\text{(common side)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle ABM\equiv\triangle ACM$ (SSS), so $\angle BMA=\angle CMA$ (matching angles).

Since $B,M,C$ lie on a straight line,
$$\begin{align*}\angle BMA+\angle CMA&=180^{\circ}\\2\angle BMA&=180^{\circ}\\\angle BMA&=90^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$
Thus $AM\perp BC$ and $BM=CM$, so $AM$ is the perpendicular bisector of $BC$. There is only one perpendicular bisector of $BC$; hence it passes through the vertex $A$.

content.prompt: $H$ and $K$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $AC$ of $\triangle ABC$. Points $H$ and $K$ are joined and the line produced to $X$ so that $HK=KX$. Prove that:

children.label: a
children.prompt: $CX$ is equal and parallel to $BH$.

answer.short:
$CX=BH$ and $CX\parallel BH$.

Use SAS congruence of $\triangle AKH$ and $\triangle CKX$, then equal alternate angles.
answer.worked:
In $\triangle AKH$ and $\triangle CKX$:

$$\begin{align*}AK&=CK\\HK&=KX\\\angle AKH&=\angle CKX\end{align*}$$

The first equality follows because $K$ is the midpoint of $AC$; the second is given; the angles are vertically opposite. Hence $\triangle AKH\equiv\triangle CKX$ (SAS).

Therefore $CX=AH$ and $\angle KHA=\angle KXC$ (matching sides and angles).

Since $H$ is the midpoint of $AB$, $AH=BH$, so $CX=BH$. The equal alternate angles $\angle KHA$ and $\angle KXC$ give $AH\parallel CX$. As $A,H,B$ are collinear, $BH\parallel CX$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: $HK=\dfrac{1}{2}BC$ and $HK$ is parallel to $BC$.

answer.short:
$HK=\dfrac12BC$ and $HK\parallel BC$.

Part a makes $BHXC$ a parallelogram, so $HX=BC$ and $HX\parallel BC$.
answer.worked:
By part a, the opposite sides $BH$ and $CX$ of quadrilateral $BHXC$ are equal and parallel. Therefore $BHXC$ is a parallelogram.

Its opposite sides give $HX=BC$ and $HX\parallel BC$.

Since $H,K,X$ are collinear, with $K$ between $H$ and $X$, and $HK=KX$:

$$\begin{align*}HX&=HK+KX\\HX&=2HK\\HK&=\frac12HX\\HK&=\frac12BC\end{align*}$$

Also, $HK$ lies on $HX$, so $HK\parallel BC$.

entries.description:
Angles of three particular sizes have special names:
• An angle of 90° is a right angle.
• An angle of 180° is a straight angle.
• An angle of 360° is a revolution.
Other angles are described by being within a range of angle sizes:
• An acute angle is an angle between 0° and 90°.
• An obtuse angle is an angle between 90° and 180°.
• A reflex angle is an angle between 180° and 360°.
For example, 30° is an acute angle, 140° is obtuse, and 220° is reflex.

entries.description:
Particular pairs of angles also have special names:
• Two angles whose sum is 90° are called complementary angles.
• Two angles whose sum is 180° are called supplementary angles.
For example, 35° and 55° are complementary angles because 35° + 55° = 90°, and 70° and 110° are supplementary angles because 70° + 110° = 180°.

entries.description:

• Adjacent angles can be added and subtracted.
• Adjacent angles on a straight line are supplementary.
• Angles in a revolution add to 360°.
• Vertically opposite angles are equal.

Angles across transversals
Suppose that a transversal crosses two lines.
• If the lines are parallel, then the alternate angles (for example, δ and γ) are equal.
• If the lines are parallel, then the corresponding angles (for example, α and β) are equal.
• If the lines are parallel, then the co-interior angles (for example, δ and β) are supplementary.

entries.description:
Isosceles and equilateral triangles
A triangle is called isosceles if it has two equal sides; it is called equilateral if all three sides are equal. Thus all equilateral triangles are also isosceles triangles.
• The base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.
• Conversely, if two angles of a triangle are equal, then the sides opposite those angles are equal.
• Each interior angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°.
• Conversely, if the three angles of a triangle are equal, then the triangle is equilateral.
Proofs of these results are reviewed in Exercise 7C.

entries.description: In ICE-EM Mathematics Year 8 we introduced the idea of congruent figures.

entries.description:
Two plane figures are called congruent if one figure can be moved on top of the other figure, by a sequence of translations, rotations and reflections, so that they coincide exactly.
Congruent figures have exactly the same shape and size.
When two figures are congruent, we can match every part of one figure with the corresponding part of the other, so that:
– matching angles have the same size
– matching paired intervals have the same length
– matching paired regions have the same area.

entries.sourceLabel: The four standard congruence tests for triangles
entries.description:
Two triangles are congruent if:
SSS: the three sides of one triangle are respectively equal to the three sides of the other triangle, or
AAS: two angles and one side of one triangle are respectively equal to two angles and the matching side of the other triangle, or
SAS: two sides and the included angle of one triangle are respectively equal to two sides and the included angle of the other triangle, or
RHS: the hypotenuse and one side of one right-angled triangle are respectively equal to the hypotenuse and one side of the other right-angled triangle.

entries.exclusionReason: Running topic band; contextual evidence only.

entries.description:
Four tests for a parallelogram
• If the opposite angles of a quadrilateral are equal, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.
• If the opposite sides of a quadrilateral are equal, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.
• If one pair of opposite sides of a quadrilateral are equal and parallel, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.
• If the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, then the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

entries.description:
The circle passing through all three vertices of a triangle is called a circumcircle of the triangle.

The following theorem not only shows that every triangle has a unique circumcircle, but also shows how to construct the circumcircle.

Prove that: The three perpendicular bisectors of a triangle are concurrent. Their point of intersection (called the circumcentre) is the centre of a circle (called a circumcircle).

Prove this theorem using congruence. In the diagram above, the midpoints of BC, CA and AB are P, Q and R respectively.

entries.description: In Exercise 7B, you proved that the sum of the exterior angles of a convex polygon is 360°. This question introduces another way of looking at this theorem.

In each diagram below, imagine that you started at the point X, facing A, and walked around the figure back to X, passing through the vertices A, B, C, … in alphabetical order. Through how many complete revolutions would you turn during your journey? Count clockwise rotation as negative, and anticlockwise revolutions as positive.

entries.description: Use these ideas to develop a proof that the sum of the exterior angles of a convex polygon is 360°.

Suppose that you make a journey on the surface of the globe. You start facing east at Singapore, which lies on the Equator. Then you walk east one-quarter of the way around the globe, then turn 90° north and walk to the North Pole, then turn 90° towards Singapore and walk back to Singapore, and finally turn facing east just as you started. Through how many revolutions have you turned during this journey, and what is the sum of the exterior angles of your triangular path?

responseRequirements: Sum of exterior angles of the triangular path
